newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Feb 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Feb 7.

text.p: TVNZ has approached the government with a proposal to sell down its stake in Clear Communications and use the proceeds to increase its shareholding in Sky Television. The network has confirmed the approach to government but says selling Clear is only one of several options to fund a possible expansion into Sky. "No decision has been made on anything, on Sky, Clear, or anything," TVNZ spokesman Alastair Carthew said. Clear chief executive Andrew Makin said he could not comment on shareholder matters. Page 1.

Aotearoa Television Network's management team is set to disintegrate. Directors of the beleagured Maori TV company were considering the future involvement of two directors, financial controller Derek Burns and Morehu McDonald, as The Independent went to press on Thursday night. On another front, senior cabinet ministers were on Thursday night still considering the results from Commerce Ministry inquiries as The Independent went to press and had not made a decision on whether to proceed with the $4 million the station needs to remain on air until June. Page 1.

Legal writs are flying in a spat over comparative advertising between personal computer retailers PC Direct and Best Buy. PC Direct is seeking damages in the High Court alleging comparative advertising by Buy Best breached the Fair Trading Act. In return Buy Best director Mark Mahony threatened to sue PC Direct for defamation after PC Direct placed full-page advertisements referring to Mahony's former failed PC company, Cost Club. The saga began when Best Buy placed advertisements late last week in the NZ Herald comparing one of its computer products with one sold by PC Direct. Page 1.

The practical benefits to gas consumers of this week's crucial and largely pro-competitive High Court decision in the long-running Kapuni case may be stymied by an exclusion clause inserted during the trial. Oil/gas producers Shell/Todd, the Kapuni plaintiffs, say a last minute offer they made to the High Court not to sell any Kapuni gas they might receive in the settlement, either for electricity generation or petrochemical use, was important if they wanted a pro-competitive settlement in their complex dispute with Natural Gas Corporation. Page 3.

The Bank of New Zealand is considering its own civil action against failed Kiwi International Airlines and/or its founder Ewan Wilson. A bank spokesman said the issue is being looked at and a decision is still to be made. Wilson appeared in the Hamilton District Court on Monday on six fraud charges related to the application he made to the Ministry of Transport in June 1995 for an international air services licence. Under the old International Air Services Licensing Act (1947) licence seekers had to prove they had adequate capital backing. In Kiwi's case, the company had to come up with $750,000. Page 3.

Aotearoa Television's board may have the power under the Companies Act to nullify the $2.4 million purchase of video and television production company 601 Digital because controversial director and former financial controller Derek Burns was involved in both sides of the transaction. Under the Act, shareholders in a company have the right to void a transaction within three months of it taking place, if one of the directors is "interested" in that transaction and the company didn't get "fair value". Aotearoa's board is seeking legal advice on this, and a number of other issues. Page 5.

While a European Community big-wig headed home with a better grasp of why New Zealand is bitching about barriers curbing the spread of spreadable butter, the government and Dairy Board were preparing for a two-pronged assault. They will challenge the EU's discrimination against spreadable butter in the European Court of Justice and at the World Trade Organisation. Page 5.

Commerce Ministry calls for an end to NZ Post's remaining postal monopoly look set to fall on deaf ears unless officials can win over NZ First. Ministry officials say NZ Post's monopoly on standard letters should be reviewed because there is a risk

efficiency gains made by the SOE will eventually be eroded. There was also potential for the company to act anti-competitively, using its protected letter-delivery business to subsidise its other businesses. The deregulation call was made in the ministry's post-election briefing to Communications Minister Maurice Williamson. Page 7.

National Bank subsidiary, Southpac Investment, is radically altering its investment management style for dealing with wholesale money. The new style combines active asset allocation -- an active choice of which sector, property, bonds, shares,

etc, to invest in and passive or index management within those sectors, buying the TeNZ index, for example. National Bank will introduce Southpac-style funds to be run alongside its existing range of actively managed products, says Financial Services deputy Graeme Kershaw. Page 6.

An outflow of $19 million in net funds was no barrier to the retail managed funds industry gaining $263 million in the last quarter. IPAC Securities' latest Industry Trends and Market Composition Report shows the funds grew on a net basis from $10.993 billion to $11.256 billion on the back of strong

investment performance, particularly in domestic equities with the NZSE40 Gross Index reporting a 10.1 percent rise. IPAC says: "a major factor was a large advisory group's allocation of investor monies from public (retail) to private funds". The group in question was Spicers Financial Services. The private funds referred to were wholesale funds, into which its in-house master trust feeds. Page 7.
